analysis.one_liner: Caps overdraft fees and bans most nonsufficient-funds fees charged by banks.
analysis.headline: The House Financial Services Committee approved the bill 27-22 on July 27, 2022, but the full House never voted on it before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would crack down on overdraft fees: banks could charge at most one overdraft fee a month and six a year per account, fees would have to be reasonable and proportional to the overdraft, and banks could no longer charge a nonsufficient-funds fee on ATM or debit card transactions. It also requires clear disclosure of fees, real-time notice when an overdraft happens, and bans a fee when the overdraft comes only from a debit hold larger than the actual purchase. The committee approved it in July 2022, but the House never took it up before the term ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who overdraw their checking accounts — disproportionately low- and moderate-income households, and disproportionately Black and Latino consumers, according to the bill's findings. Anyone who has paid a $35 fee to cover a $4 coffee would pay fewer such fees, get warnings before a transaction triggers one, and see fees capped.

how_it_helps.text: Caps overdraft coverage fees at one per calendar month and six per calendar year per account, and requires fees to be reasonable and proportional to the overdraft amount and the bank's cost of providing coverage.
Prohibits banks from charging any nonsufficient fund fee on ATM or debit card transactions, and bars a fee when an overdraft results solely from a debit hold larger than the actual transaction.

Requires banks to disclose overdraft fees in all marketing, get written consent before charging fees on ATM and point-of-sale overdrafts, notify consumers the same day overdraft coverage is used, and offer the chance to cancel a teller or ATM transaction that would trigger a fee.

Requires banks to post transactions in an order that minimizes overdraft and nonsufficient-funds fees, and bars reporting negative overdraft information to credit bureaus when the overdraft and fees are repaid under the program.
Imposes a one-year moratorium on overdraft and nonsufficient-funds fee increases starting at enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Banks and credit unions, which collect billions of dollars a year in overdraft and nonsufficient-funds fees, much of it from account holders with low balances. If banks cut back overdraft coverage or free checking in response, some consumers could lose access to a service they relied on.

drawbacks.text: The fee caps and ban on ATM and debit-card nonsufficient-funds fees cut off a large revenue stream banks say helps fund free checking accounts and other account services, so some banks could respond by raising other fees, adding minimum-balance requirements, or reducing account access for people with low balances.

Banks retain discretion to simply refuse to pay overdrafts, so a consumer whose coverage is capped at one fee per month and six per year could see later transactions declined rather than covered, turning a $35-fee problem into a bounced-payment problem in some cases.
The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau would need to write implementing rules within 24 months, which adds regulatory burden and delay before consumers see the benefits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary consumers the benefits are direct and concrete: fewer overdraft fees, warnings before triggering one, honest disclosure, and protection from fees caused purely by debit holds. The main cost falls on banks, not consumers, though a real risk exists that banks offset lost fee revenue with other fees or tighter account access. The one-fee-per-month cap could also push some repeat overdraft users into declined transactions. On balance the bill is squarely aimed at a fee practice that falls hardest on people with the least money.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared the House Financial Services Committee in a 27-22 vote in July 2022, but no further action was ever taken and it died when the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced June 30, 2021 and referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.
On July 27, 2022 the committee held a markup and voted 27-22 to order the bill reported, in the nature of a substitute, as amended.
The bill was never reported to the House floor and received no vote in the full House; the action history ends with the committee vote and the Congress ended January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks and credit unions that collect overdraft and nonsufficient-funds fees — revenue that can run into the billions of dollars a year — are better off because the bill never became law. Consumers continue paying overdraft fees at the old rates.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Banks that collect overdraft fee revenue

sides.party_line_note: All 66 cosponsors were Democrats, and the committee vote to advance the bill went 27-22, splitting on party lines in the Democratic-majority committee; the bill never reached the full House for a recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill caps overdraft fees at one per month and six per year, requires them to be reasonable and proportional, bans ATM and debit-card nonsufficient-funds fees, and freezes fee increases for a year. Overdraft and nonsufficient-funds fees fall disproportionately on low-balance account holders, so the industry's interest in keeping the fees runs against consumers here.

The bill amends the Federal Credit Union Act to count overdraft coverage fees as finance charges, subjecting credit unions to the same fee caps, disclosure, and ban on nonsufficient-funds fees as banks.

The bill bars banks from reporting negative overdraft information to consumer reporting agencies when the overdraft and fees are repaid, reducing the data those agencies hold and the damage overdrafts can do to a consumer's file.
